newsitem.title: FRANCE: Rebuffed LVMH to try to lead investor revolt.
newsitem.headline: Rebuffed LVMH to try to lead investor revolt.

text.p: LVMH said on Friday it would focus on building support among Guinness and Grand Metropolitan shareholders after the two British companies rejected LVMH chairman Bernard Arnault's proposals.

"Moet Hennessy Louis Vuitton is not surprised. We knew the managements did not like our plan," an LVMH spokeswoman said in Paris, adding "we will pursue our strategy of explaining our plan to investors and shareholders".
Brokers and analysts say the fight could drag on for months after Guinness and GrandMet dashed any hope on Friday of a negotiated settlement.
"We're going to war," said Olivier Blitz at Paris brokerage IFF. "But the market has faith in Arnault."
LVMH shares were steady in early Friday trade but weakened by midday, easing 0.43 percent in a market that rose 0.8 percent.
The luxury group has spent some 12 billion francs ($1.9 billion) in cornering an 11.06 percent stake in GrandMet in its bid to line up enough votes to block a merger between GrandMet and Guinness.
This stake was paid for through the sale of Guinness shares, and on Thursday it sold a further two million shares in the Irish group, reducing its holding to 12.2 percent from 12.3 percent.
"If push comes to shove, Arnault will liquidate his Guinness holding to buy GrandMet," said a London-based analyst.
Analysts say he is focusing on GrandMet because the company requires 75 percent shareholder approval for the merger. At Guinness only a simple majority is needed.
"The only thing Arnault can do is to keep seeing investors and portfolio managers to try to convince them that his plan is superior and to get them to vote with him," another industry analyst said.
Arnault was in London marketing his plan to investors on Thursday.
Analysts say investors are attracted by Arnault's argument that the drinks, food and brewing businesses would be better off if they were managed separately.
However, some disagreed with the British groups' claim that GMG Brands would become a multi-product consumer brands group like Colgate-Palmolive or Procter & Gamble.
Arnault wants the British companies to de-merge their brewing and food businesses and form a three-way drinks merger.
One analyst with a French brokerage said Arnault may force the British groups back to the negotiating table if he can line up enough support among GrandMet shareholders.
"No one really wants the merger scrapped because the premium is already priced into Guinness and GrandMet shares," the analyst said.
Arnault, a tough boardroom battler, effectively controls LVMH. An Arnault family holding indirectly owns 25 percent of LVMH and controls over 40 percent.
